steps.label: Conclusion (Thus)
steps.body: The new screening test can prompt dangerous operations that actually are not medically necessary.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The new screening test detects some polyps that turn out not to be malignant, but doctors usually have them surgically removed, which is a dangerous process.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion is weakly worded. It only claims the new test can prompt dangerous operations that are not medically necessary.

Do we know the test leads to dangerous operations? Close enough. It finds polyps so early that it is generally unclear whether they are malignant, and in most cases doctors have such polyps surgically removed anyway. The researcher tells us that removal is a dangerous process.

Do we know those operations are not medically necessary? Not quite. The evidence only says some of the polyps "turn out not to be malignant." The author treats that as if it means the surgery was "not medically necessary." That is the leap. Maybe a polyp that is not malignant still needs to come out for some other medical reason.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer expressing the author's linking move: at least some of the time, removing a polyp that turned out not to be malignant was not medically necessary.

Or look for an answer ruling out the objection we just built, something like this: nonmalignant polyps don't always need to come out for some other medical reason.

Either way, negate it. If the negation lets us say every one of these operations was medically necessary after all, we've found the assumption.

notes.body: The argument is about medical necessity, not ethics. Negate A: a dangerous operation can be ethically justified even when the condition it treats is not more dangerous. The researcher can accept that and still say some of these polyp removals were not medically necessary, so the argument survives.

The evidence says some removed polyps turn out not to be malignant. The conclusion says some of the operations were not medically necessary. B is the bridge between those two terms: removing a nonmalignant polyp is not always medically necessary.

Negate it: surgical removal of nonmalignant polyps detected by the test is always medically necessary. Now every operation the test prompts was needed, malignant or not, and the conclusion has nothing left to stand on. The negation wrecks the argument, so the argument requires B.

Notice the soft wording. "Not always" only asks for some unnecessary removals, which is exactly as much as "can prompt" in the conclusion needs. On a necessary assumption question, a modest answer that connects the evidence's term (not malignant) to the conclusion's term (not medically necessary) is the shape to look for.

C tells us what to do about the test: stop using it or change it. The argument stops earlier, at the claim that the test can prompt unnecessary operations. Negate C: even if the test encourages unnecessary operations, it should still be used as is. The conclusion is untouched, because it never said what to do next.

D is about malignant polyps, and the gap is about the ones that are not malignant. Negate it: some malignant polyp found by the test should not be removed. That tells us nothing about whether removing a nonmalignant polyp is necessary, so the argument is unaffected.

The argument never measures how useful the test is. Negate E: the test is medically useful even when it finds polyps that need no treatment. The researcher can agree and still say the test can prompt unnecessary surgery. "Only when" makes E a strong claim the argument has no use for.

note: Notes are sound; replaced the loose kept Evaluate step (it said "Not yet" about operations the stimulus says happen in most cases and put an invented thought in quotation marks), removed quotation marks from an invented Goal prediction, and made the A negation exact ("not more dangerous").

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body:
These tablets challenge the widely held belief among historians that the Sumerian civilization in Mesopotamia was the first to create literature.
rephrase: it seems like someone created literature earlier than the Sumerians in Mesopotamia

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Recently discovered clay tablets from southern Egypt date to between 3300 and 3200 B.C.
One of them appears to contain literary writing.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion has a conspicuous new term: the Sumerian civilization in Mesopotamia. The evidence only tells us about Egyptian tablets dated to between 3300 and 3200 B.C.

For those tablets to challenge the belief that the Sumerians were first, historians must not already credit the Sumerians with literature from before the tablets. If historians believed the Sumerians were writing literature in 3500 B.C., an Egyptian tablet from 3300 B.C. would come in second, and there would be nothing to challenge.

Try an everyday version. Jerry can bench press 200 lbs. Hence, this accomplishment challenges the widely held belief among students that Maggie is the strongest student in school. What are we assuming about Maggie? That the students don't already think Maggie lifts more than 200 lbs. If they believed Maggie benched 250, Jerry's lift would change nothing.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying historians don't date the Sumerians' first literature before the Egyptian tablets, in other words, not earlier than about 3300 B.C. Negate it, and the tablets arrive too late to challenge anything.

notes.body: The argument already has its literary tablet: one translated tablet appears to contain literary writing. Negate A: most of the untranslated tablets do not contain literature. That one literary tablet is still there, so the challenge stands. More literary tablets would help, but the argument doesn't need them.

B links tax records to other kinds of writing, but the argument never reasons from the tax records. It has direct evidence: a tablet that appears to contain literary writing. Negate B: some civilization kept tax records and nothing else. The argument loses nothing, because it rests on the literary tablet.

C fills the gap we predicted. The evidence dates the literary tablet to between 3300 and 3200 B.C. The conclusion says this challenges the belief that the Sumerians were first. That only works if historians don't already place Sumerian literature earlier than the tablet.

Negate C: historians generally believe the Sumerians did create literature earlier than 3300 B.C. Then the Egyptian tablet comes second on the historians' own timeline, and it challenges nothing. The argument falls apart, so C is required.

The move to repeat: when the conclusion brings in something the evidence never mentioned (here, the Sumerians), the assumption usually connects that new term to the evidence. Ask what must be true about the new thing for the evidence to matter.

D would hurt the argument, not hold it up. Negate it: no historians are skeptical about the tablets' authenticity. That only makes the evidence look better. A necessary assumption is something whose denial damages the argument, and denying D helps it.

E dates when Sumerian civilization arose, but the belief in question is about when the Sumerians first created literature. A civilization can exist for centuries before anyone writes literature. Negate E: the civilization arose at some other time, say 4000 B.C. The argument still works as long as Sumerian literature came after the tablet.

note: Logic and notes are correct (C is required, the 3200 B.C. overstatement and pronouns are fixed); only removed quotation marks from the invented Jerry/Maggie analogy so no quoted text is non-bank wording.

steps.label: Given that
steps.body: Captive leatherbacks are exposed to fatal diseases they'd never encounter in the wild.

steps.label: How can it be that
steps.body: The likelihood of reaching maximum life expectancy is about the same in captivity and in the wild?

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
We're told there's something worse / life-shortening about living in captivity.

So if the odds of reaching max life expectancy are the same for captive vs. wild, then we need to hear one of these:
- something good / life-elongating about captivity
- something bad / life-shortening about the wild
- these fatal diseases that become a risk in captivity are not actually shortening the lives of very many leatherbacks

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: I'd be looking for a distinction between captivity and the wild, something GOOD about captivity or BAD about the wild, when it comes to life span.

notes.body: A compares leatherbacks with other large aquatic reptiles. The surprise is a comparison between captive leatherbacks and wild ones. Fewer diseases attacking leatherbacks would be true in both places, so it creates no difference between captivity and the wild that could offset the captivity diseases.

B compares sea turtles with other marine animals, which is the wrong comparison. Even if sea turtles live long in general, that is true of captive and wild leatherbacks alike, so it doesn't explain why the extra diseases in captivity fail to lower the captive odds.

This is the something-bad-about-the-wild answer we predicted. Captive leatherbacks face diseases the wild ones never meet. Wild leatherbacks face predators, and C tells us predators kill most of the wild ones that perish. Captive turtles are presumably safe from predators. So each setting has its own main danger, and the odds of reaching full life expectancy can come out about the same.

The move to repeat: when two groups end up equal even though one has an obvious disadvantage, look for a disadvantage on the other side that balances it.

D deepens the paradox. If few zoologists know how to build an environment that is good for captive leatherbacks, captivity sounds even worse for them. That is one more reason to expect captive turtles to die younger, which is the opposite of what we need.

E might tempt you if you suspect the life-expectancy figures are measured badly. But nothing in E says the error affects captive and wild turtles differently. If size is a poor guide to age everywhere, it gives no difference between the two settings, so the surprise remains.

note: Notes are correct and now give real reasons; only removed quotation marks around a self-quoted prediction that is not bank wording (and does not even match the Goal step exactly).

steps.label: Given that
steps.body: Patients in private rooms generally get fewer infections and shorter stays than patients in semiprivate rooms.

steps.label: How can it be that
steps.body: Woodville's hospital has only semiprivate rooms, yet its infection rates and stays match nearby hospitals with mostly private rooms and very similar patients?

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: The patients are similar, so look at how the rooms are used. A semiprivate room is built for two, but if Woodville often puts only one patient in it, its patients get the benefit of a private room.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find a difference between Woodville and the nearby hospitals that gives Woodville's patients the benefits of private rooms.

notes.body: A gives us a similarity: many of the same doctors work at Woodville and at the nearby hospitals. We need a difference that gives Woodville's patients the benefit of private rooms. Shared doctors are the same on both sides, so they can't explain why a hospital with only semiprivate rooms keeps up with hospitals that are mostly private.
We want a reason why Woodville is doing better than we'd expect, and being told that it is an older hospital seems more to be a reason why it would do worse than one might expect.

This is reinforcing the background claim, explaining why private rooms tend to lead to lower infection rates and shorter hospital stays.
It does nothing to explain the surprise, which is why Woodville's semiprivate rooms seem to be doing as well as other hospitals' private rooms.

We want a reason Woodville's semiprivate rooms do as well as other hospitals' private rooms, and this gives it.

If Woodville puts one patient in each semiprivate room whenever it can, then in practice many of its patients get a room to themselves. So Woodville gets the benefits of private rooms without having any, and the surprise goes away.
E does give a difference, location, but nothing ties being downtown to fewer infections or shorter stays. To make E work we'd have to invent that link ourselves, so the surprise is still standing.

note: D note overclaimed "most" patients from "whenever possible" (now "many"), and the E note wrongly implied a resolution must be about the rooms; both trimmed, rest approved.
Two-comparison setup is correct, D trap note correctly fixes the old error (D does explain honey vs. cleaning-only, not honey vs. ointment), no dashes or misquotes.
Evaluate now predicts the rule-reason-missing-in-exception move, C note teaches it, wrong notes give real reasons, quotes exact.

steps.label: Given that...
steps.body: On the plains where it lives, an individual zebra stands out because of its black-and-white stripes, which contrast with the green or brown of the surrounding vegetation. Zebras are a prey species, and the lions that hunt them can see stripes clearly.

steps.label: How can it be that...
steps.body: Zebras survive with such vivid markings.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The stimulus closes the obvious escape route. The stripes contrast with the green or brown vegetation, and lions can see stripes clearly. So the stripes don't hide zebras. They seem to announce to every lion that lunch is right here.

So how does a zebra survive with them? Seeing a zebra isn't the same as catching one. The stripes could protect zebras in some way other than hiding, for example during the chase. Or zebras could have some other protection that makes up for being easy to spot.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that the stripes help zebras survive in some way other than making them hard to see, such as making them harder to catch once a lion attacks. A weaker but possible version would give zebras some other defense that offsets being visible.

notes.body: A tells us true camouflage would have to change with the seasons. Zebra stripes don't change, so A only confirms that zebras aren't camouflaged. It says nothing about how a zebra that stands out still survives.

B says zebras can tell which lions are preparing to hunt and ignore the others. That might save some wasted running, but it doesn't make a zebra any harder to catch once a lion does hunt, and the lion still spots the zebra easily. Any prey animal could have this skill, so B gives no reason a zebra this visible gets away.

C makes things worse for zebras. Lions blend in with dry vegetation and can creep close before attacking. A hidden hunter going after easy-to-see prey should succeed more often, which deepens the puzzle about how zebras survive.

D is about what lions do after a kill. Sharing the food doesn't change how often lions bring down a zebra, and it has nothing to do with the stripes. The puzzle about surviving with vivid markings is untouched.

E gives the stripes a job other than hiding. Zebras generally run in a group when danger comes, and in a running group the stripes make it hard for a predator chasing one zebra to discern its outline. A lion can spot the herd easily but struggles to keep track of the one zebra it is chasing.

That resolves the puzzle. The stimulus showed the stripes don't help a zebra hide. E shows they help it escape. Being seen and being caught are two different things, and E works in that gap.

The move to repeat: when the stimulus rules out the obvious benefit (here, camouflage), look for an answer where the same feature helps in another way.

note: Writer-flagged B note overclaimed that B does not help zebras escape at all and leaned on "nothing to do with the stripes" though the Goal allows another defense; rewrote it to say B does not make a visible zebra harder to catch, and removed an invented quote (Simba) from the Evaluate step.

steps.label: Given that ...
steps.body: Rainwater is almost totally pure and thus should be expected to dilute polluted seawater when it falls onto Crystal Bay.

steps.label: How can it be that ...
steps.body: Shortly after a heavy rainfall, pollution levels in Crystal Bay reach their highest levels?

steps.label: Evaluate / Goal
steps.body: We need a way to explain how rain, or something that accompanies rain, is adding pollution to Crystal Bay. Maybe when it rains heavily, people in this town light more fires in their fireplace, and the smoke from the fireplace drifts over the Bay and drops particulates on the water, adding to its pollution levels. Who knows. Let's just find some way to connect heavy rainfall to pollution in the Bay.

notes.body: A explains why the rain's diluting effect would be tiny: there isn't much rainwater compared with the bay. A tiny dilution means pollution should stay about the same. But the pollution goes up, to its highest levels. A explains why the rain doesn't help, not why pollution rises.

B gives the connection we were looking for. Most of the rainwater that reaches Crystal Bay first falls on pesticide-treated fields. It picks up pesticides there and carries them into the bay. A heavy rainfall means a lot of runoff and a lot of pesticide arriving at once, so pollution peaks shortly after.

The move to repeat: this paradox quietly assumed the rain goes straight into the bay. When a fact seems to point one way (pure water should dilute), ask what happens between that fact and the result. Here the rain picks up pollution on the way.

C is about where the water in rain clouds comes from. Whatever its origin, the stimulus tells us the rain is almost totally pure. Where the water started gives no way for heavy rain to add pollution to the bay.

D names the bay's leading pollution source, beachgoers' trash that blows into the bay. But nothing in D ties that trash, or the wind that carries it, to rainfall. A pollution source with no stated link to rain can't explain why the peak comes shortly after a heavy rainfall.

E says nearby ocean areas show an extremely similar pattern of pollutant increase and decrease. Suppose that pattern includes the same spike after rain. Then the puzzle has spread to more places, and we still don't know why rain raises pollution anywhere. A repeated pattern is not an explanation of it.

note: Writer-flagged D note rested on an outside guess (fewer beachgoers in rain); replaced with the text-based reason that D never links the trash to rainfall, and added a missing comma in the kept Evaluate step.
